biography: Son of Francis Kyd, a London scrivener; baptized 6 November 1558. Probably attended Merchant Taylors' School. Little is known of his life before The Spanish Tragedy (c. 1587), which made his name. In May 1593 he was arrested after papers denying the deity of Christ were found in his lodgings; he claimed they belonged to Christopher Marlowe, his former room-mate, and was tortured in Bridewell. He died in August 1594, buried on 15 August, in debt and obscurity.
literary_profile: Author of the most influential revenge tragedy of the age, The Spanish Tragedy (c. 1587), with its play-within-the-play, its ghost of Don Andrea, and its hero Hieronimo; also wrote the tragedy Soliman and Perseda (c. 1592) and Cornelia (1594), a translation of Robert Garnier's Senecan tragedy, and is the probable author of the lost ur-Hamlet.
stylistic_characteristics: Senecan rhetoric, ghosts and revenge choruses, dramatic irony, the device of the play within the play, and a blank verse line of strong end-stops that Marlowe and Shakespeare both learned from.
intellectual_concerns: Justice and its frustration; the morality of private revenge; the theatre's power to reveal concealed crime.
historical_significance: The founding figure of English revenge tragedy; The Spanish Tragedy was the most popular play of its generation and shaped Hamlet and a hundred imitations.
biographical_uncertainty: Almost nothing certain about his education; the ur-Hamlet attribution is probable but not proven; several minor plays have been conjecturally assigned to him.

biography: Grandson of William Lily the grammarian; educated at Magdalen College, Oxford (BA 1573, MA 1575). His Euphues (1578) made him famous overnight. From 1583 he wrote court comedies for the Children of Paul's and the Children of the Chapel, and sat in Parliament four times. He spent years petitioning in vain for the post of Master of the Revels and died in relative poverty, buried 30 November 1606.
literary_profile: Inventor of Euphuism — the antithetical, allusion-laden prose style of Euphues: The Anatomy of Wit (1578) and Euphues and His England (1580) — and author of the elegant court comedies Campaspe (1584), Sapho and Phao (1584), Gallathea (c. 1588), Endymion (1588), Midas (1589), Mother Bombie (c. 1590), and Love's Metamorphosis (c. 1590).
stylistic_characteristics: Euphuism: balanced antitheses, elaborate similes drawn from the natural histories of Pliny, proverbial wisdom, and a polished, self-conscious wit carried into his prose-like dramatic dialogue.
intellectual_concerns: The education and conduct of the courtier; the claims of love against the claims of state; the language of power and persuasion.
historical_significance: His prose style dominated fashionable writing for a decade and his court comedies laid the foundation of high English comedy; Shakespeare parodied and absorbed him in equal measure.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate; some plays are dated conjecturally from performance records.

biography: Baptized 11 July 1558 in Norwich; took his BA at St John's College, Cambridge (1580) and MA from Clare Hall (1583), and was incorporated at Oxford. He came to London to live by the pen, married, abandoned his wife, and died in poverty on 3 September 1592 after a banquet of Rhenish wine and pickled herring, leaving the deathbed pamphlet Greene's Groatsworth of Wit, which contains the notorious 'upstart Crow' attack on Shakespeare.
literary_profile: The most prolific of the University Wits: plays include Alphonsus, King of Aragon (c. 1588), Friar Bacon and Friar Bungay (c. 1589), James IV (c. 1590), and Orlando Furioso (1591); romances include Pandosto (1588), the source of The Winter's Tale, and Menaphon (1589); pamphlets include the cony-catching series (1591–92) exposing the tricks of London's underworld.
stylistic_characteristics: Euphuistic prose, romantic plotting, pastoral charm, and a pamphlet style of vivid, confessional journalism.
intellectual_concerns: The moral and financial perils of authorship; repentance; the underworld of London; the rivalries of the professional stage.
historical_significance: A central University Wit whose romantic comedy and prose fiction fed Shakespeare directly; his cony-catching pamphlets are landmarks of English prose realism and rogue literature.
biographical_uncertainty: His repentances were staged for the press; the Groatsworth attribution is generally accepted though its circumstances are murky.

biography: Baptized 25 July 1556; son of the clerk of Christ's Hospital. Educated at Christ's Hospital and Broadgates Hall (later Pembroke College), Oxford, where he took BA (1577) and MA (1579). He came to London in the early 1580s, wrote for the public stage and the City, and dissipated his talents and health; he was buried on 9 November 1596.
literary_profile: His pastoral-mythological court play The Arraignment of Paris (c. 1581–84) pleased Elizabeth; The Old Wives' Tale (c. 1591–93) is a folkloric comedy of enchantment; The Battle of Alcazar (c. 1588–89) and Edward I (c. 1590) are chronicle plays; he also wrote Lord Mayor's pageants and the biblical tragedy David and Bethsabe (c. 1594).
stylistic_characteristics: Lyrical sweetness, Ovidian ornament, and a gift for pageantry and stage spectacle; the famous 'garden speech' in the anonymous play sometimes assigned to him shows his fluent, decorative blank verse.
intellectual_concerns: Court compliment and civic ceremony; classical myth reworked for English audiences.
historical_significance: A pioneer of the history play and of polished stage verse; traditionally credited with a share in Shakespeare's Titus Andronicus.
biographical_uncertainty: The extent of his share in Titus Andronicus remains debated; his canon is the most unstable among the Wits.

biography: Baptized November 1567 at Lowestoft; son of a curate. BA from St John's College, Cambridge (1586). He came to London about 1588 and earned a living by the pen, often in hardship. He fought the pamphlet war with Gabriel Harvey in the 1590s, fled London after the scandal of The Isle of Dogs (1597), and died in or about 1601, aged thirty-three.
literary_profile: Pierce Penniless His Supplication to the Devil (1592), The Unfortunate Traveller (1594) — the first picaresque novel in English — the anti-Puritan satire Christ's Tears over Jerusalem (1593), the play Summer's Last Will and Testament (1592, printed 1600), the erotic poem The Choice of Valentines, and the lost Isle of Dogs (1597), co-written with Ben Jonson, which closed the London theatres by order of the Privy Council.
stylistic_characteristics: Furious verbal energy: colloquialism mixed with learned allusion, compound coinages, mock-heroic rhetoric, and the fastest, funniest prose of the decade.
intellectual_concerns: The condition of authorship without patronage; the hypocrisy of Puritans and pedants; urban poverty and plague; the grotesque body.
historical_significance: The great prose satirist of the 1590s and a pioneer of English fiction; his prose style was absorbed by Jonson, Dekker, and the pamphleteers who followed.
biographical_uncertainty: Death date approximate; the circumstances of his last years are obscure.

biography: Born near Hitchin about 1559; studied at Oxford but left without a degree, then served in the Low Countries. He began writing for the theatre around 1594 and completed Marlowe's Hero and Leander in 1598. His great labour was the translation of Homer: the Iliad (1598–1611) and Odyssey (1614–15), which Keats would celebrate in the sonnet 'On First Looking into Chapman's Homer'. He died in London on 12 May 1634.
literary_profile: Plays include The Blind Beggar of Alexandria (1596), the two-part Bussy D'Ambois (c. 1604), The Conspiracy and Tragedy of Charles, Duke of Byron (1608), Eastward Ho (1605, with Jonson and Marston, which landed its authors in prison for satire of the Scots), and The Widow's Tears (c. 1605); his verse includes the philosophical poem The Shadow of Night (1594) and Ovid's Banquet of Sense (1595).
stylistic_characteristics: A dense, oracular style — packed conceits, stoic sententiae, a 'dark' obscurity his contemporaries mocked but which carries his tragedies of heroic aspiration.
intellectual_concerns: Stoic virtue; the heroic individual against the court; Neoplatonic theories of inspiration and learning.
historical_significance: His Homer fixed the English reading of the epics for two centuries, and his tragedies of Bussy D'Ambois and Byron are the fullest English expression of the heroic, Senecan mode.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate; his claims of gentility and a university degree are unproven.

biography: Son of a prosperous London coachmaker and member of the Merchant Taylors' Company; born about 1580. He entered the Middle Temple about 1598 and began collaborating with Dekker and others (Westward Ho, 1604; Northward Ho, 1605) before the independent tragedies that made his name. Nothing is known of his last years; he was dead by about 1634, when Heywood called him 'that worthy poet' in the past tense.
literary_profile: The White Devil (1612), The Duchess of Malfi (c. 1614), The Devil's Law Case (c. 1619), and Appius and Virginia (c. 1626, with Heywood); his famous character essays were appended to the 1615 Overbury collection.
stylistic_characteristics: A poetry of darkness: lurid emblems, macabre wit, great set-piece dirges, and a sombre moral seriousness beneath the sensational surface.
intellectual_concerns: Corruption of courts; the abuse of women by rank and power; the gulf between appearance and worth; death as the great leveller.
historical_significance: With The Duchess of Malfi he wrote what many rank the greatest non-Shakespearean tragedy of the English stage; his heroines and villains shaped the Jacobean imagination.
biographical_uncertainty: Both birth and death dates approximate; almost all personal details are inferred from records of the Coachmakers' Company and the Middle Temple.

biography: Baptized 18 April 1580 in London; son of a bricklayer who left a comfortable estate. He matriculated at Queen's College, Oxford, in 1598 but left without a degree to write for the theatre. From 1613 he wrote the annual Lord Mayor's pageants, and in 1620 was appointed City Chronologer. His political allegory A Game at Chess (1624) — a satire on the Spanish match — became the greatest box-office success of the age and provoked a diplomatic uproar. He died at Newington Butts and was buried 4 July 1627.
literary_profile: The most versatile of the Jacobean professionals: city comedies (A Mad World, My Masters, 1605; A Trick to Catch the Old One, c. 1605; A Chaste Maid in Cheapside, 1613), tragedies (Women Beware Women, c. 1621; The Changeling, 1622, with Rowley; and — by the current consensus of attribution — The Revenger's Tragedy, 1606), and the political satire A Game at Chess (1624).
stylistic_characteristics: Swift, sardonic wit; a fascination with money, appetite, and the mechanics of deceit; ferocious tragic irony; and a moral disgust that never blunts his comic energy.
intellectual_concerns: The corruptions of City and court; marriage as property transaction; the ethics of revenge; political and religious controversy.
historical_significance: The second great dramatist of the Jacobean age after Shakespeare and Jonson; A Game at Chess is a landmark of political theatre.
biographical_uncertainty: The attribution of The Revenger's Tragedy has shifted from Tourneur to Middleton on stylistic evidence; much of his output was collaborative and shares are sometimes disputed.

biography: Born in London about 1572, probably of Dutch descent. He began writing for Henslowe's companies in 1598 and was imprisoned for debt in the Poultry Counter (1598–99). He collaborated with nearly every dramatist of the age — Jonson, Marston, Webster, Middleton, Ford, Massinger — and wrote some of the period's most vivid plague pamphlets. He died on 25 August 1632, still in debt.
literary_profile: Plays include The Shoemaker's Holiday (1599), Old Fortunatus (1599), Satiromastix (1601, with Marston, in the war of the theatres against Jonson), The Honest Whore (1604–05, with Middleton), and The Witch of Edmonton (1621, with Ford and Rowley); prose includes The Wonderful Year (1603) and The Gull's Hornbook (1609).
stylistic_characteristics: Warmth, sentiment, and a Londoner's ear for the trades and cries of the city; his best scenes have a lyrical realism unmatched by his contemporaries.
intellectual_concerns: The dignity of citizens and craftsmen; plague and providence; the cheerful endurance of poverty.
historical_significance: The great celebrant of London's citizens; The Shoemaker's Holiday remains the most performed city comedy of its generation, and his pamphlets are major documents of urban life.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate; little is known of his family and education.

biography: Born about 1575, of obscure family. He served in military and diplomatic posts — in the Low Countries, and as secretary to the council of war in the Cadiz expedition of 1625. On the return voyage he fell ill and was put ashore at Kinsale, Ireland, where he died on 28 February 1626.
literary_profile: Certainly his are the morality-influenced tragedy The Atheist's Tragedy (1611) and the elegy A Grief on the Death of Prince Henry (1613); The Revenger's Tragedy (1606–07) was long printed under his name but is now generally assigned to Middleton.
stylistic_characteristics: Senecan rhetoric pressed toward allegory and emblem; a satiric, almost allegorical handling of revenge and atheism.
intellectual_concerns: The punishment of atheism; the workings of providence; revenge and its ironic reversals.
historical_significance: His name remains attached to one of the masterpieces of Jacobean tragedy, even as scholarship has transferred the play itself to Middleton.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date and parentage unknown; the Revenger's Tragedy attribution is now disputed and generally given to Middleton.

biography: Baptized 7 October 1576; son of a lawyer of the Middle Temple, where he himself was admitted in 1592. He took his BA at Brasenose College, Oxford, in 1594. He wrote verse satires and plays for the boy companies, fought the war of the theatres with Jonson (who caricatured him in Poetaster), then abruptly left the stage in 1608, took holy orders in 1609, and spent his last years as rector of Christchurch, Hampshire. He resigned his living in 1631 and died in London on 25 June 1634.
literary_profile: Verse satires The Scourge of Villainy and The Metamorphosis of Pygmalion's Image (1598); plays include Antonio and Mellida (c. 1599–1600), Antonio's Revenge (c. 1600), The Malcontent (1604), The Dutch Courtesan (1605), and Eastward Ho (1605, with Chapman and Jonson).
stylistic_characteristics: A deliberately harsh, snarling satiric style — neologism, paradox, and a bitter wit aimed at courtly vice and poetic affectation alike.
intellectual_concerns: The exposure of vice; malcontentedness as a moral stance; the corruption of the court and the law.
historical_significance: The malcontent he created in The Malcontent became one of the defining types of Jacobean drama and inspired Shakespeare's and Webster's handling of the figure.
biographical_uncertainty: The reasons for his abrupt retirement from the theatre are unknown.

biography: Born in 1584 to a prominent Leicestershire legal family; his brother was the poet Sir John Beaumont. He entered Broadgates Hall, Oxford, in 1597 and the Inner Temple in 1600, but the law gave way to the theatre. From about 1606 to 1613 he collaborated with John Fletcher in one of the most celebrated partnerships in literary history, living with him in Bankside 'in the same house and bed'. He married an heiress in 1613, retired to Kent, and died on 6 March 1616; he is buried in Westminster Abbey.
literary_profile: With Fletcher he wrote Philaster (c. 1609–10), The Maid's Tragedy (c. 1610–11), A King and No King (1611), and The Knight of the Burning Pestle (c. 1607), the brilliant mock-romance that failed on its first production; his unaided works include the verse epistle to Jonson and the poems in the 1618 collection.
stylistic_characteristics: Wit, metrical suppleness, and a taste for burlesque and self-conscious theatricality; the Beaumont–Fletcher canon is noted for its tragicomic design and its courtly polish.
intellectual_concerns: The ethics of honour and friendship; the conventions of romance and their parody; the relation of the stage to its audience.
historical_significance: Half of the partnership whose plays dominated the stage for fifty years after Shakespeare's death; Beaumont–Fletcher tragicomedy defined the Caroline and Restoration taste that followed.
biographical_uncertainty: The exact division of labour between Beaumont and Fletcher in each play is unknown and much debated.

biography: Baptized 20 December 1579 at Rye; son of Richard Fletcher, later Bishop of London. He was educated at Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, and probably began writing for the stage about 1606. After his partnership with Beaumont he collaborated with Shakespeare (Henry VIII, The Two Noble Kinsmen) and with Massinger, and in 1616 succeeded Shakespeare as principal dramatist of the King's Men. He died of the plague in August 1625 and is buried in Southwark Cathedral.
literary_profile: Sole and collaborative canon of some fifty plays, including The Faithful Shepherdess (c. 1608), The Woman's Prize (c. 1611), The Island Princess (c. 1621), Rule a Wife and Have a Wife (1624), and, with Beaumont, Philaster, The Maid's Tragedy, and A King and No King.
stylistic_characteristics: Supple, flowing blank verse with feminine endings; rapid plotting; a taste for surprise, disguise, and the reversals of tragicomedy.
intellectual_concerns: Honour, love, and friendship under pressure; the follies of tyranny; the pleasures of wit and gallantry.
historical_significance: His fluent verse and tragicomic plots set the pattern for Restoration drama; for the next half-century 'Beaumont and Fletcher' outran even Shakespeare at the box office.
biographical_uncertainty: Shares in the fifty-play canon are often uncertain; the Beaumont–Fletcher division of labour remains debated.

biography: Baptized 24 November 1583 at Salisbury; son of a gentleman servant to the Herbert family. He studied at St Alban Hall, Oxford (1602–06), then went to London and collaborated with Fletcher, Dekker, and Field. After Fletcher's death in 1625 he became chief dramatist of the King's Men. He died suddenly on 17 March 1640 at his house on the Bankside and was buried in Fletcher's grave in Southwark Cathedral.
literary_profile: Some thirty plays survive, including The Roman Actor (1626), The City Madam (c. 1632), A New Way to Pay Old Debts (c. 1625), and The Bondman (1623); he completed Fletcher's unfinished work and wrote many plays in partnership.
stylistic_characteristics: Careful construction, political earnestness, and a moral seriousness that made his comedies satires on greed and his tragedies studies of tyranny.
intellectual_concerns: The abuse of power; the corruption of wealth; justice and mercy in the state.
historical_significance: The last major dramatist of the pre-Civil War stage; his Sir Giles Overreach in A New Way to Pay Old Debts became one of the great actor's roles of the English repertoire.
biographical_uncertainty: A period of obscurity and possible religious conversion (he was reputed a Catholic) in the 1610s is poorly documented.

biography: Born in Lincolnshire about 1573; studied at Emmanuel College, Cambridge. He was acting and writing for Henslowe's companies by 1598 and claimed to have had 'an entire hand, or at least a main finger' in 220 plays. He wrote pageants, translations, and compendious works of history and mythology, and died in Clerkenwell on 16 August 1641, one of the last survivors of the great Jacobean generation.
literary_profile: A Woman Killed with Kindness (1603), the domestic tragedy The English Traveller (c. 1627), the four-part Ages cycle (1611–32), The Fair Maid of the West (c. 1600), and the prose An Apology for Actors (1612), the period's chief defence of the stage.
stylistic_characteristics: Plain, humane, middle-style verse; domestic settings; moral plots of patience and repentance that avoid the lurid excesses of his rivals.
intellectual_concerns: The dignity of the ordinary household; marital betrayal and forgiveness; the moral legitimacy of the theatre.
historical_significance: His domestic tragedy founded a genre that runs through Lillo to Ibsen; An Apology for Actors is the classic defence of the English stage.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the vast collaborative canon makes his exact share in many plays uncertain.

biography: Born 22 January 1561 at York House, London; son of Sir Nicholas Bacon, Lord Keeper. Educated at Trinity College, Cambridge, and Gray's Inn, he rose under James I to Attorney General (1613), Lord Keeper (1617), Lord Chancellor (1618), and Viscount St Alban (1621), then fell in 1621 on charges of corruption, was fined and briefly imprisoned, and spent his last five years in philosophical retirement at Gorhambury. He died on 9 April 1626 of bronchitis contracted while stuffing a chicken with snow to test refrigeration.
literary_profile: The Essays (1597; enlarged 1612 and 1625), The Advancement of Learning (1605), Novum Organum (1620), the utopian New Atlantis (1626, published 1627), and the History of the Reign of King Henry VII (1622), together with a mass of legal, scientific, and political writings.
stylistic_characteristics: Aphoristic compression, balanced antithesis, and the deliberate plainness of a mind committed to lucid exposition; his Essays made the form an English genre.
intellectual_concerns: The reform of learning; induction and the interpretation of nature; the uses of knowledge for power and charity; the conduct of public life.
historical_significance: The chief English spokesman of the new science and the maker of the English essay; his vision of organized inquiry shaped the Royal Society and the Enlightenment that followed.
biographical_uncertainty: The circumstances of his fall are still debated by historians; the 'Baconian' claims about Shakespeare's works are rejected by scholarship.

literary_identity: theologian; apologist of the Church of England
biography: Born at Heavitree near Exeter in early April 1554. Educated at Corpus Christi College, Oxford, he became a fellow, then Master of the Temple in 1585, where his famous controversy with the Puritan Walter Travers sharpened his defence of the established church. He became rector of Bishopsbourne in Kent, where he completed his great work; he died on 3 November 1600, cared for by his friend Lancelot Andrewes.
literary_profile: Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity — Books I–IV published 1593, Book V in 1597, and Books VI–VIII posthumously — the classic reasoned defence of the Elizabethan settlement against Puritan attack.
stylistic_characteristics: Majestic, periodic prose of extraordinary clarity and dignity, argued with a sweet reasonableness that Izaak Walton celebrated and that set the standard for English theological prose.
intellectual_concerns: The relation of law, reason, and scripture; the nature of the church and of civil society; the grounds of political obligation.
historical_significance: The intellectual foundation of the Anglican via media; his theory of law and government influenced Locke and the mainstream of English constitutional thought.
biographical_uncertainty: The authorship of the later books of the Polity is complicated by posthumous editing; parts of the last three books survive imperfectly.

biography: Born at Boston, Lincolnshire, in 1516 or 1517. Educated at Brasenose and Magdalen College, Oxford, he resigned his fellowship over religious scruples, tutored in the households of the Protestant gentry, and fled to the Continent under Mary I, working at Basel as a proofreader for the printer Oporinus. He returned under Elizabeth and spent his later years as a preacher and writer in London, where he died on 8 April 1587.
literary_profile: Actes and Monuments of These Latter and Perilous Days — the 'Book of Martyrs' — first published in English in 1563 and greatly expanded in 1570, a vast church history built around the sufferings of Protestant martyrs from Wyclif to his own day.
stylistic_characteristics: Massive documentary accumulation, vivid narrative set-pieces, and the rhetorical urgency of a man writing the history of his own cause.
intellectual_concerns: Providence in history; the true church against Antichrist; the testimony of the martyrs.
historical_significance: His book, ordered to be placed in every cathedral church, shaped English national and religious identity for three centuries and is a primary source for the Marian persecutions.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date uncertain (1516 or 1517).

biography: Born in 1536 at Buckhurst, Sussex; educated at Oxford (Inner Temple, and Cambridge). He entered Parliament in 1558 and rose through the law and the council to become Baron Buckhurst (1567), a commissioner at the trial of Mary Queen of Scots, and Earl of Dorset and Lord Treasurer (1599–1608). He died suddenly at the council table at Whitehall on 19 April 1608.
literary_profile: Co-author with Thomas Norton of Gorboduc (performed 1561–62), the first English tragedy in blank verse, and author of the great 'Induction' and the 'Complaint of Henry Duke of Buckingham' contributed to A Mirror for Magistrates (1563), which he planned and edited with others.
stylistic_characteristics: Grave, stately, Senecan moral verse; the Induction's descent into the underworld is the finest English poetry between Chaucer's death and Spenser.
intellectual_concerns: The dangers of a divided succession; the falls of princes; counsel and the commonwealth.
historical_significance: Gorboduc founded English tragedy and political drama; the Mirror for Magistrates he fathered became the great poetic storehouse of Elizabethan tragedy.
biographical_uncertainty: The exact division of the Gorboduc acts between Sackville and Norton is unknown.

biography: Born about 1539 at Cardington, Bedfordshire, into a landed family; educated at Trinity College, Cambridge, and Gray's Inn. He sat in Parliament, served in the Low Countries campaigns, and was captured by the Spanish at Leiden in 1574. He died on 7 October 1577 at Stamford, having returned home to revise his works.
literary_profile: A Hundred Sundry Flowers (1573) — including the prose fiction The Adventures of Master F.J. — The Posies (1575), the satiric mirror poem The Steel Glass (1576), the plays Supposes (1566, from Ariosto) and Jocasta (1566, from Euripides via Italian), the hunting manual The Noble Art of Venery (1575), and the first English treatise on verse, Certain Notes of Instruction (1575).
stylistic_characteristics: Experimentation across every available form — prose fiction, satire, drama, sonnet, blank verse — with a confessional, self-advertising wit.
intellectual_concerns: The reform of English versification; the moral uses of satire; the politics of courtly advancement.
historical_significance: The first great professional man of letters in English — innovator of the sonnet, the essay-like miscellany, and the English blank-verse drama from Italian models.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the autobiographical readings of Master F.J. remain contested.

literary_identity: balladeer; prose fiction writer; silk weaver
biography: A silk weaver by trade, probably born in Norwich about 1560. He became the most popular ballad-maker of his generation; several of his broadsides offended the authorities, and he was briefly in trouble over a ballad on the scarcity of grain in 1596. He died in 1600, apparently in poverty, leaving the fiction on which his later fame rests.
literary_profile: The prose narratives Jack of Newbury (1597), The Gentle Craft (c. 1597–98), and Thomas of Reading (c. 1600), which turned the lives of English craftsmen and merchants into popular fiction, together with hundreds of ballads of which a handful survive.
stylistic_characteristics: Plain, vigorous, humorous prose full of proverbs, workman's lore, and the speech of shop and street; a bourgeois realism new to English fiction.
intellectual_concerns: The dignity and prosperity of trade; the pleasures of the middling sort; charity, industry, and honest dealing.
historical_significance: The first English novelist of the working people; his fictions reached a readership far below the court and founded the tradition of popular prose romance.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date and birthplace approximate; his surviving ballad canon is a fraction of a much larger lost output.

biography: Born in London in 1558, son of a Lord Mayor of London. Educated at Merchant Taylors' School and Trinity College, Oxford, he turned to literature, travelled to the Canaries and South America, then converted to Catholicism and took up medicine, graduating MD at Avignon in 1600. He practised in London until his death of the plague in September 1625.
literary_profile: The romance Rosalynde (1590) — the direct source of Shakespeare's As You Like It — the euphuistic romance Euphues' Shadow (1592), the mythological poem Scilla's Metamorphosis (1589), the satires A Fig for Momus (1595), the play The Wounds of Civil War (c. 1588), and the translation of Josephus (1602).
stylistic_characteristics: Euphuism softened into pastoral lyricism; a fluent, musical prose of courtship, disguise, and greenwood virtue.
intellectual_concerns: Pastoral retreat and its therapeutic power; love and loyalty; the quarrel between poetry and the professions.
historical_significance: Through Rosalynde he gave Shakespeare one of his richest sources and helped fix the English pastoral romance as a form.
biographical_uncertainty: The dates and details of his travels are reconstructed from allusions in his own works.

biography: Born about 1552, probably in London; educated at Westminster School and Christ Church, Oxford, where his vocation was fixed when he saw a world map in his cousin's chamber. He lectured on geography at Oxford, served as chaplain to the English embassy in Paris (1583–88), and became rector of Wetheringsett, archdeacon of Westminster (1603), and a promoter of the Virginia enterprise. He died on 23 November 1616 and is buried in Westminster Abbey.
literary_profile: Divers Voyages Touching the Discovery of America (1582) and the great The Principal Navigations, Voyages, Traffics and Discoveries of the English Nation (1589; vastly expanded 1598–1600), the documentary epic of English overseas enterprise.
stylistic_characteristics: Editor rather than stylist: an unrivalled assembler of first-hand narratives, translated and arranged with patriotic purpose and scholarly care.
intellectual_concerns: The expansion of England; trade, colonization, and Protestant rivalry with Spain; the practical sciences of navigation and geography.
historical_significance: 'The prose epic of the modern English nation' (Froude); his collections became the sourcebook of English imperialism and shaped the language's sense of the world.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date and birthplace approximate.

biography: Born about 1554 at Hayes Barton, Devon. He fought in France and Ireland, rose at court through the favour of Elizabeth I, and was knighted in 1585. He organized the attempted Roanoke colony and expeditions to Guiana. After Elizabeth's death he was convicted of treason on flimsy evidence and imprisoned in the Tower (1603–16), where he wrote his History of the World. Released for the disastrous Guiana voyage of 1617, he was executed on 29 October 1618 on the old sentence.
literary_profile: The Discoverie of the Large, Rich and Beautiful Empire of Guiana (1596), the History of the World (1614), the Cynthia poems ('The Ocean to Cynthia' fragments), and lyrics such as 'The Lie', 'The Passionate Man's Pilgrimage', and the poem written the night before his death.
stylistic_characteristics: A grave, plain, sententious style in prose; in verse, an introspective melancholy unusual in the Elizabethan court lyric.
intellectual_concerns: Fortune and the fall of greatness; colonial wealth and its moral cost; providence and the vanity of human glory.
historical_significance: The embodiment of the Elizabethan adventurer-intellectual; his History of the World was read for its stoic grandeur, and his myth has haunted English literature ever since.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the canon of his shorter poems rests on early anthologies and is partly uncertain.

biography: Born in London in 1553, son of Michelangelo Florio, an Italian Protestant exile. He taught Italian to the court and nobility, served in the household of the Earl of Southampton, became reader in Italian to Queen Anne (1604), and groom of the privy chamber (1619). A friend of Jonson and Samuel Daniel, he died of the plague at Fulham in October 1625.
literary_profile: His Italian–English dictionaries A World of Words (1598) and Queen Anna's New World of Words (1611), the dialogue manuals First Fruits (1578) and Second Fruits (1591), and above all the translation of Montaigne's Essays (1603), one of the great translations in the language.
stylistic_characteristics: A florid, expansive English that enlarges Montaigne's French into the idiom Shakespeare knew; a tireless coiner and collector of words.
intellectual_concerns: The transmission of Continental learning; language as national wealth; scepticism and the essay form.
historical_significance: His Montaigne gave English thought and letters — including Shakespeare's Tempest — direct access to the Essays, and his dictionaries record the Italian loan-words entering Elizabethan English.
biographical_uncertainty: His role as possible editor for Southampton's circle remains a matter of speculation.

literary_identity: translator; soldier; justice of the peace
biography: Born 28 May 1535 in London, younger son of Edward North, 1st Baron North. Educated at Peterhouse, Cambridge, and Lincoln's Inn, he saw military service in Ireland and the Low Countries and later sat as a justice in Cambridgeshire. He died about 1603.
literary_profile: The Dial of Princes (1557, from Guevara via French) and the Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans (1579) — his translation of Plutarch from Jacques Amyot's French, which became the single most important non-dramatic source for Shakespeare's Roman and Greek plays.
stylistic_characteristics: A full, energetic, idiomatic English prose of remarkable dramatic vividness; Shakespeare followed it so closely that whole passages of the plays are North's sentences re-lined as verse.
intellectual_concerns: The exemplary lives of great men; counsel and conduct; the translation of classical wisdom for English readers.
historical_significance: North's Plutarch is the most consequential translation of the English Renaissance, the quarry of Julius Caesar, Coriolanus, Antony and Cleopatra, and Timon of Athens.
biographical_uncertainty: Death date approximate; the records of his last years are scanty.

biography: Born about 1536, half-brother of Margaret Golding, mother of the Earl of Oxford. Educated perhaps at Jesus College, Cambridge, he served in the household of Sir William Cecil and translated steadily through the 1560s and 1570s, chiefly from the classics and from Calvin. He died in May 1606.
literary_profile: The translation of Ovid's Metamorphoses — the first four books in 1565, the complete fifteen in 1567 — together with versions of Caesar, Justin, Seneca, and Calvin's sermons and treatises; his Ovid is 'Shakespeare's Ovid' and the Renaissance Englishman's classic.
stylistic_characteristics: Energetic fourteeners (rhymed seven-stress couplets) that render Ovid with moralizing commentary and a homespun vividness; Puritan in gloss, pagan in gusto.
intellectual_concerns: The reconciliation of classical myth with Protestant morality; the edification of the common reader.
historical_significance: His Metamorphoses made Ovid an English book and fed Shakespeare, Spenser, and the entire mythological vocabulary of the Elizabethans.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate; details of his education are uncertain.

biography: Born at Leeds about 1580, younger son of Sir Thomas Fairfax of Denton. He lived as a scholarly country gentleman, devoted to translation, and died on 27 January 1635. His fame rests on a single book.
literary_profile: Godfrey of Bulloigne, or the Recovery of Jerusalem (1600) — his translation of Tasso's Gerusalemme Liberata into English ottava rima — together with twelve eclogues printed in 1631 and a lost history of Edward the Black Prince.
stylistic_characteristics: A grave, musical, deliberate verse that renders Tasso's romance-epic with fidelity and grace; Dryden judged him the equal of the best translators.
intellectual_concerns: The heroic ideal; the claims of romance against epic; English verse as a fit medium for Italian poetry.
historical_significance: His Tasso is the great English version of the Italian epic tradition and a landmark of translation as an art.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate; his lost works are known only by report.

biography: Born in Kent in 1563, son of a clothier. He was educated at King's School, Southampton, and worked as a merchant and secretary, spending much of his life on the Continent in the service of the Merchant Adventurers. He died at Middelburg in the Netherlands on 28 September 1618.
literary_profile: Du Bartas His Divine Weeks and Works — his translation of Guillaume de Saluste du Bartas's biblical epic La Sepmaine, published piecemeal from 1592 and complete in 1608 — the most widely read religious poem of its generation after the Bible.
stylistic_characteristics: Copious, inventive, heavily figured verse that renders du Bartas's cosmological baroque with gusto; a diction of striking coinages that fed Milton's word-hoard.
intellectual_concerns: The creation and providential order of the world; sacred poetry as the highest calling; Protestant piety in verse.
historical_significance: His Du Bartas was a schoolbook of the seventeenth century and a formative influence on the young Milton.
biographical_uncertainty: The chronology of his foreign service is imperfectly known.

biography: Born 8 February 1577 at Lindley, Leicestershire. Educated at Brasenose and Christ Church, Oxford, where he spent his life as student, tutor, librarian of Christ Church, and vicar of St Thomas's. A recluse among books, he died on 25 January 1640, having predicted his own death by horoscope; he is buried in Christ Church Cathedral.
literary_profile: The Anatomy of Melancholy (1621; five expanded editions in his lifetime, with a sixth posthumous in 1651), the vast encyclopedic treatise-disguised-as-self-cure written under the name 'Democritus Junior'.
stylistic_characteristics: A prose of endless quotation, digression, and cataloguing — learned, humane, and often hilarious — that turns a medical treatise into a labyrinthine anatomy of everything.
intellectual_concerns: Melancholy in all its causes and cures; the vanity of learning; love, religion, and the passions as diseases of the mind.
historical_significance: A summa of Renaissance psychology and a fountainhead for Sterne, Lamb, and the whole tradition of English digressive prose.
biographical_uncertainty: Almost all knowledge of his character comes from the book itself and from Anthony Wood's memoir.

biography: Born in the parish of St Michael Cornhill, London, about 1525, son of a tallow-chandler. A tailor by trade, he gave up the craft for antiquarian study, publishing chronicles and surveys on which he spent his modest means. In old age he was licensed to beg, and he died in poverty on 6 April 1605; his monument stands in St Andrew Undershaft.
literary_profile: The Survey of London (1598; enlarged 1603), the loving topographical description of the city, and A Summary of English Chronicles (1565), the basis of his larger Annales (1580, 1592).
stylistic_characteristics: Plain, affectionate, accumulative prose — the voice of a man walking his city street by street, ward by ward, remembering what was there before.
intellectual_concerns: The preservation of civic memory against Reformation destruction and urban change; the antiquity and honour of London.
historical_significance: The Survey is the foundation of London historiography and an irreplaceable record of the pre-Fire city.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate.

biography: Born 2 May 1551 in the Old Bailey, London. Educated at Christ's Hospital and St Paul's School, then at Magdalen and Christ Church, Oxford. He taught at Westminster School (1575–97), where his pupils included Ben Jonson, and ended his career as Clarenceux King of Arms (1597). He died on 9 November 1623 at Chislehurst, Kent.
literary_profile: Britannia (1586, in Latin; English translation by Philemon Holland, 1610), the chorographical description of Britain, and the Annales of the reign of Elizabeth I (1615–25).
stylistic_characteristics: Exact, methodical, elegant Latin and an English style of grave plainness; the scholar's impartiality joined to patriotic purpose.
intellectual_concerns: The recovery of British antiquity; the writing of sober, documented history against legend; national identity through the past.
historical_significance: The father of English antiquarianism; his Britannia launched the great tradition of county and national history that runs through the seventeenth century and beyond.
biographical_uncertainty: The accuracy of the Annales on some episodes is disputed by later historians.

biography: Born at Thaxted, Essex, about 1577. Educated at St John's College, Cambridge, he took orders and served as chaplain and rector, most notably of St Martin Ludgate, London. He inherited Richard Hakluyt's unpublished papers and made them the core of his great collection. He died in 1626, probably in London.
literary_profile: Purchas His Pilgrimage (1613) and Hakluytus Posthumus, or Purchas His Pilgrimes (1625), the four-volume folio that continued and crowned Hakluyt's work of collecting the world's voyages.
stylistic_characteristics: Compilatory and devout: he arranges others' narratives within a providential frame, adding moral reflection and apology for his 'pilgrimage' through the world's records.
intellectual_concerns: The spread of the Gospel and of English trade; the world as theatre of providence; the preservation of voyages from oblivion.
historical_significance: His Pilgrimes preserved many accounts that survive nowhere else and helped form the English colonial imagination in the seventeenth century.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate.

biography: Baptized 27 January 1569 in London, daughter of Baptist Bassano, a court musician of Italian origin. After her father's death she became the mistress of Henry Carey, Lord Hunsdon, the Lord Chamberlain; later she married the court musician Alfonso Lanyer. In 1611 she published Salve Deus Rex Judaeorum, making her one of the first Englishwomen to issue a volume of poetry in her own name. She died on 3 April 1645.
literary_profile: Salve Deus Rex Judaeorum (1611) — a long poem on Christ's Passion with a proto-feminist 'Eve's Apology' and the defence of women's learning, prefaced by dedicatory poems to a roll-call of great ladies and followed by 'The Description of Cooke-ham', the first country-house poem in English.
stylistic_characteristics: Devotional narrative in rhyme royal with a distinctively woman-centred exegesis; a grave, ornate, occasionally magnificent handling of biblical story.
intellectual_concerns: Women's virtue, learning, and agency; the Passion and its female witnesses; patronage among women.
historical_significance: A founding voice of English women's poetry; 'Eve's Apology' is the first sustained feminist argument in English verse, and Cooke-ham precedes Jonson's Penshurst in the country-house genre.
major_influences: Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke
biographical_uncertainty: Her relationship with Shakespeare, if any, is the stuff of speculation, not record; the Forman casebooks document her consultations but their readings are contested.

biography: Born in 1587, eldest daughter of Robert Sidney of Penshurst and niece of Sir Philip Sidney and of Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke. In 1604 she married Sir Robert Wroth of Loughton, Essex, who died in 1614 leaving her with debts and a small child. Her long affair with her cousin William Herbert, Earl of Pembroke, was the scandal behind her fiction. She died about 1651 or 1653.
literary_profile: The Countess of Montgomery's Urania (1621) — the first prose romance by an Englishwoman, a continuation of her uncle's Arcadia — with its appended sonnet sequence Pamphilia to Amphilanthus, and the pastoral closet drama Love's Victory (c. 1620, circulated in manuscript).
stylistic_characteristics: A Sidneyan inheritance — pastoral romance, interlaced plots, and sonnets of constancy — transformed by a woman's perspective on love's costs to women.
intellectual_concerns: Female constancy and male inconstancy; the politics of marriage; women's authorship and its risks.
historical_significance: The first Englishwoman to write a prose romance and a sonnet sequence; the outcry over Urania's court portraits shows the reach of her fiction.
major_influences: Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke
biographical_uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; Love's Victory circulated in manuscript and its dating is inferred.

biography: Born 7 September 1533 at Greenwich, daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn. Educated by Roger Ascham and others in the new humanist curriculum, she became queen in 1558 and reigned until her death on 24 March 1603 at Richmond Palace. Her learning, her speeches, and her poems made her one of the most literate monarchs in English history.
literary_profile: Poems including 'The Doubt of Future Foes' (c. 1571), 'On Monsieur's Departure' (c. 1582), and 'When I Was Fair and Young'; translations from Boethius, Horace, and Plutarch made in her youth; prayers and meditations; and the great public orations — the speech at Tilbury (1588) and the 'Golden Speech' to Parliament (1601).
stylistic_characteristics: A pointed, antithetical, proverbial style in verse and a commanding rhetorical art in her speeches, learned and plain by turns.
intellectual_concerns: Kingship and its burdens; marriage, succession, and the body politic; divine protection and personal constancy.
historical_significance: Her speeches and poems made the queen herself a literary presence; the cult of Elizabeth pervades Spenser, Shakespeare, and the entire literature of her reign.
biographical_uncertainty: A few poems are assigned to her by tradition rather than manuscript authority.
